newsitem.title: USA: U.S. governors divided over welfare changes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. governors divided over welfare changes.

text.p: U.S. governors opened their winter meeting on Saturday quarreling over a federal cutoff of aid to legal immigrants under a new welfare law and vowing to oppose a White House plan to cap annual Medicaid spending.

Governors spent much of Saturday trying to work out a compromise that could provide more money to states that will lose billions of dollars under the welfare law, which ends Food Stamps and disability aid to most legal immigrants.
But they were deeply divided about how far the National Governors' Association (NGA) should go on the issue.

An NGA working group put together a draft policy, to be voted on during the four-day meeting, to exempt the elderly and disabled and those seeking citizenship from the cutoff, if they were in the United States before the law took effect.
The compromise only partly restores aid to immigrants, who will begin losing federal benefits this summer.

"We will have chaos in the state when we cut off benefits to people who are legally there," said Florida Democratic Gov. Lawton Chiles, whose state has a huge immigrant population. "It is totally unfair ... this is the mother of all unfunded mandates."

Some Republican governors said on Saturday they did not support the draft policy, calling it unwise to reopen the welfare law over an issue that affected relatively few states. They added they were hopeful they could work out a compromise.

"I don't want to open it up and I don't want to cause problems so Congress doesn't give us more responsibility on other (issues)," said Wisconsin Republican Gov. Tommy Thompson, whose state has been a leader in welfare efforts.
Behind the scenes, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, has worked to mute any call by the NGA for a major revamping of the immigrant policy.

Lott has complained that states asked for broad authority under the welfare law and must be willing to accept it. He is also worried about money. The immigrant cutoff saves $24 billion over six years, money Republican leaders need to help reach a balanced budget deal.
"We don't have a surplus and we don't have a rainy day fund (like the states). We have a big national debt and an annual deficit that we're trying to address," Lott said this week.
Vermont Democratic Gov. Howard Dean said Republican governors were "under enormous pressure from their friends on (Capitol) Hill" on the issue.
President Bill Clinton's 1998 budget proposal, which he will send to Congress on Thursday, will include billions of dollars to restore aid to legal immigrants.

The NGA draft policy on immigration would require up to $1.5 billion in additional federal spending each year. Iowa Republican Gov. Terry Branstad suggested the NGA should instead set up a special block grant to aid states.

The sour, defensive tone was in stark contrast to the NGA meeting a year ago when state executives asked Congress to give them broad control over a host of federal programmes, including welfare and the Medicaid health programme for the poor, elderly and disabled.

Only six months after Clinton signed the welfare law, governors also said they would likely ask Congress to change some of its work requirements and ensure a five-year time limit on welfare applies only to cash aid and not other benefits.

Governors appear united on another contentious issue: Medicaid. Both Democrats and Republicans said the NGA would oppose any plan by Clinton to cap funding for the Medicaid programme for 37 million poor, elderly and disabled Americans.

"All of us are joined at the hip and opposed to the caps, Republican and Democrat. If the president and Congress put caps on Medicaid it would devastate our state budgets," said Ohio Republican Gov. George Voinovich.

Clinton's budget is expected to call for annual limits on Medicaid spending. Medicaid is an open-ended entitlement, jointly funded by state and federal governments. The programme has been the fastest growing part of many state budgets, comprising about 20 percent of state spending on average.
The governors did win one victory. Environmental Protection Agency administrator Carol Browner said she would seek an extra 60 days to review proposed air quality standards.

EPA's proposals to tighten restrictions on allowable levels of smog-producing ozone and airborne particulates have come under fire from businesses and many state officials worried about the cost of the proposed new restrictions.
